video_title: Verging on Another Escalation in the Middle East | Ali Vaez
transcript: What's up, everybody? My name is Dimitri Kofinas, and you're listening to Hidden Forces, a podcast that inspires investors, entrepreneurs, and everyday [music] citizens to challenge consensus narratives and learn how to think critically about the systems of power shaping our world. My guest in this episode of Hidden Forces is Ali Vaez, deputy program director for the Middle East and North Africa at the Crisis Group, and one of the most closely watched analysts of [music] Iran's foreign and nuclear policy. Ali played a direct role in the negotiations that produced the 2015 nuclear deal that the Trump administration withdrew from in 2018. By the end of today's conversation, you will have a clearer understanding of where the war between Iran and the United States actually stands 8 months following the commencement of Operation Epic Fury, how Iran [music] has turned its control of the Strait of Hormuz into a tool for pressuring the global economy, what this conflict has caused Washington, Tehran, and their respective allies, and why the window for a durable diplomatic solution may be closing, and what an escalation of hostilities would look like for the region, its geopolitics, and the global economy. Ali and I spend the first hour of our conversation establishing the state of play 8 months [music] into Operation Epic Fury, how the war has metastasized into a wider regional confrontation involving the Houthis in Yemen and attacks on Saudi Arabia, and what the fighting has cost the United States military, including a significant depletion of its missile interceptor stockpiles and the loss of several regional bases. We also discuss how the war has reshaped Iran's internal politics, economy, and society, and why coordination between Washington and Tel Aviv appears to be breaking down. The second hour is devoted to a conversation about how the United States and its Gulf allies [music] have kept oil flowing through the Strait of Hormuz despite Iran's blockade, and why that workaround is not sustainable. We also discuss how Iran's national security doctrine has shifted since the war began, the state of its nuclear ambitions, the degradation of Western intelligence networks [music] inside the country, and what a new, more durable security architecture for the Middle East might require, including whether any of this is achievable before this war ends, whether it will take a new administration in the White House to see it through. If you want access to all of this conversation, go to hiddenforces.io/subscribe [music] and join our premium feed, which you can listen to on your mobile device using your favorite podcast app, just like you're listening to this episode right now. If you want to join in on the conversation and become a member of the Hidden Forces Genius community, which includes Q&A calls with guests, discounted access to third-party research and analysis, and in-person events like our intimate dinners and weekend [music] retreats, you can also do that on our subscriber page. And if you still have questions, feel free to send an email to info@hiddenforces.io, [music] and I or someone from our team will get right back to you. And with that, please enjoy this timely and deeply informative conversation with my guest, Ali Vaez. Ali Vaez, welcome to Hidden Forces. >> Great pleasure to be with you. >> The pleasure is all mine, Ali. It's great having you on the show. I've been reading your work in Foreign Affairs and Foreign Policy magazine and the New York Times, among other publications, and I've been following you on Twitter for some time. So, I'm excited to finally get you on the show. I don't want to assume that everyone already knows who you are. You're the deputy program director at the Crisis Group for Middle East and North Africa. So, give us a little bit of a sense of your background. How did you become an expert on Iranian affairs, and what is the nature of your foreign policy experience? >> Well, it's actually a peculiar story, and I I don't want to get too much into its details, but I just shared the basics with you. Interestingly, I've actually published this in Foreign Affairs. I had an essay in 2023. It's called The Long Twilight of the Islamic Republic, in which I intertwine my personal story because I actually studied pure sciences, biotechnology, and nuclear physics. That's where I got my master's and PhD, and even I did a postdoc in pure sciences until 2009, when I decided, all of a sudden, to completely shift gears and come into the policy world. But, I realized I didn't have the technical background, and so I went to get another master's degree in international relations in DC, and that's how I switched. So, I came out of school in DC in 2011, which coincided with a very dark period in US-Iran relations, with nuclear negotiations ongoing and anywhere, and the risk of war being pretty high. And I decided that I if there's anything I could do to try to prevent another conflict between Iran and the US or the US committing another mistake of engaging in another war in the Middle East, I should. And I kind of got lucky because in 2012, I was hired by Crisis Group, and immediately I had fantastic access to policymakers in every key stakeholder countries. And in 2013, diplomacy became much more serious between Iran and the US, and I could have direct impact on the negotiations, which led eventually in 2015 to the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, JCPOA. So, that's the main story of me getting involved in foreign policy from science, but it has I've had a lot of ups and downs throughout this process. You know, when I started working on nuclear negotiations, I thought this is it. This is how people from the nonprofit world, from the outside of government, can have direct impact on policy. And that you could do really good things. I didn't realize that that was sort of an exception to the rule, which is that a lot of stars will have to align for think tankers and policy experts to be able to have direct impact on policy. And that often the cost and the frustrations of being involved in this process are so much more than the feeling of being impactful. >> Or that the agreement would be negated so quickly. How many years did you guys actually work on that agreement? >> Crisis Group was involved from the beginning of this crisis in 2003. We had a president, Gareth Evans, who was the former foreign minister of Australia and a very well-known nonproliferation expert. He's also the author and the originator of the idea of responsibility to protect. And the core bargain of the JCPOA, which is nuclear restrictions and transparency measures in return for economic incentives, was really his idea that was put on the table in 2003. So, the organization's been involved in and out throughout the years until I I got involved. And then we were very intimately consulted by all sides. The whole process of JCPOA negotiation, I would say, took about 2 and 1/2 years. It did survive for almost around the same period of time, 2 and 1/2 years. It was implemented in January of 2016, and President Trump withdrew from it in May of 2018. And you know, Iran stayed in it for another year even after the US withdrew and reimposed sanctions. By that point, the deal was already an empty shell. So, 2 and 1/2 years to negotiate, 2 and a half years to fall apart. >> So, we're nearing 8 months since the commencement of Operation Epic Fury and the constriction of commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. We have seen multiple reported ceasefire negotiations collapse and have since seen the war expand to the Red Sea with attacks by Houthi forces in Yemen, including devastating missile and drone and strikes against Riyadh in Saudi Arabia and Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and King Fahd International Airport on the Persian Gulf. What is the state of the war at this moment? >> Well, it is a metastasizing conflict on the one side and it's a stalemate on the other. A metastasizing in the sense that the Yemen dimension of this has already gained a life of its own that is, I would say, independent now of what would happen between Iran and the US. You can imagine all sorts of scenarios of escalation or de-escalation between Iran and the US that would not necessarily affect the dynamics in Yemen. It might, but it also might not. But when it gets to Iran and the US, we are in an absolute state of stalemate. There were efforts on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York about 3 weeks ago, end of September, to try to figure out if there is a way of getting Iran and the US back to the negotiating table. The Qatari mediators tried very hard. The Iranians came with a new proposal that would basically condense the timeline that they had agreed to with the US in a memorandum of understanding that both sides signed on to back in June to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in 30 days. The Iranians put a proposal on the table that would do so in 7 days. And the concept was that they were hoping that a condensed timeline would be attractive to President Trump because it would get to open the strait and bring down energy prices prior to the midterms, but my sense was that they were also realistic enough that that's probably not going to work because Washington's optimism about what sanctions could achieve and what the renewed pressure that the US has been imposing on Iran in the past few weeks, not just in the form of a naval blockade, but also almost a air blockade and much tougher enforcement of existing sanctions would eventually bring Iran to its knees. And so the Iranians also did this putting proposal on the table in order to win both the international blame game that they are not the inflexible party at fault, but also to demonstrate to their own people that they are trying to find a solution and if they can't, it's because the US is in pursuit of maximalist demand. The US wanted Iran to include a nuclear concession in that package. And therefore, you know, the deal would be different than what was negotiated in June because the president is clearly I think the criticism about the June MOU got under his skin that this was a deal that was very favorable to the Iranians. And so he was trying to get something that would be different. The problem on the Iranian side is that if they agree to a different deal and they would put additional concessions on the table, they are afraid that that would send the wrong message to Washington. That pressure is working and that's why Iranian position has become more accommodating of US demand and that's why we're in a stalemate. So that means there is a risk that either the Iranians would try to mount an October surprise by escalating in a way that would allow them to break this blockade and the economic pressure that the US is putting on them or that the US would do so either to give the president a victory in the run-up to the mid-terms or right after the mid-terms when he would have very little to lose because the outcome would be what it is. >> So, your response raised a number of questions about how the war is actually going and what effect it's had on the various counterparts. Before we assess the impact on Iran or America's force posture in the region or how it's disrupted commercial traffic and what Washington has done to try to mitigate that, I do have at least one more question about the Saudi experience because the bombings I mentioned in my last question have happened only in the last few days. When is the last time that Saudi Arabia experienced anything like this? And how bad have these attacks been? >> Well, the Saudis did experience cross-border attacks, a lot of drones and missiles fired by the Houthis during the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis from 2015 to 2022. But then they had a ceasefire agreement with the Houthis in Yemen and since then there was relative quiet across the border. And in 2023, the Saudis also normalized relations with Iran after similar period of tensions from 2016. The relations were cut off until 2023. And that's helped as well to keep that conflict quiet and the Saudis and the Emirates not being directly affected. So, you're right. This is now after several years quite a bit of shock to the Saudis, especially given how effective the Houthi targeting has been against civilian targets like the Riyadh airport. >> I mean, I'm familiar with cases where Saudi civilian infrastructure has been attacked, notably 2017, but I don't recall those attacks being as significant as what we're seeing now. >> Well, there were some airports that had been attacked, but not Riyadh airport, and especially not a case in which we had significant number of casualties including an American. >> So, how do these attacks on Saudi Arabia complicate the war for Washington? >> Well, it complicates the war in several ways in the sense that, you know, at this point, President Trump will have to decide whether he would break the ceasefire agreement that the US has with the Houthis as of last spring. For 2 months, the US last spring bombed the Houthis. It was a significant escalation, but the Houthis fired back and especially at US naval assets in the Red Sea, and the US lost several high-tech fighter jets. remember exactly they were F-15s or F-35s, but in any case, it was a significant loss of assets and was very costly undertaking. And at that point, the president pragmatically pulled the plug on the continuation of that confrontation. I remember in the Biden administration when the US was bombing the Houthis, somebody asked President Biden whether he thinks the bombing would work. He said, "No, but we will continue doing it." And that's the real lesson of bombing the Houthis from the air, that it was done by Saudi-led coalition for 7 years, it was done by the Biden administration, it was done by the Trump administration, it has not worked. And it will not work. Even ground forces, the Yemeni government forces been mobilized and have retaken some of the territory that the Houthis have conquered over the past few weeks. They can't really roll back the gains that the Houthis have had especially through the control of the capital and in Sana'a. So, there is a limit to what could be achieved militarily against the Houthis, and I think President Trump learned that lesson last But now, if he doesn't do anything and decides that he wants to keep the ceasefire with the Houthis, it will be seen as a betrayal by Gulf allies, especially the Saudis. And it would diminish US credibility. So, it's damned if you do and damned if you don't in this case. But, if there is a new front open and the US enters into the conflict, I would say that would generally work pretty well for the Iranians. Because then the US would have to protect its naval assets who could come under fire from two different directions, both from the Iranians and from the Houthis. And I remind you that several weeks ago, the Iranians did successfully fire a warning shot towards one of US warships that was in Indian Ocean. And finding that vessel and getting through its very sophisticated air defense system to detonate a anti-ship cruise missile in and of itself is quite a military feat, but the Iranians did it in order to send a warning to the Trump administration of what would happen if the economic pain on Iran would become too sharp. Now, having the Houthis aligned with them and firing at the Americans would be a gift to the Iranians. But again, the other side of the coin which is not doing anything for the Trump administration is not attractive either. >> Does that kind of effective targeting suggest that the Iranians are getting support, maybe from the Chinese, as has been reported? >> Oh, 100%. It's either the Chinese satellites imagery or Russian intelligence, but undoubtedly, the Iranians have become better at targeting US naval assets and could not do it on their own without support from other great powers like China or Russia. >> How much cooperation and coordination is there between the Houthis and the Iranians or are the Houthis just simply taking advantage of this window of opportunity to gain more territorial control over Yemen. >> So, these two are not mutually exclusive in the sense that the Houthis are primarily driven by their own agenda. They were unhappy with the fact that the Saudis had imposed a blockade on the ports and on the airports and wanted to find a way of getting out of that deadlock. And we're looking for a pretext, we're preparing for another round of confrontation with Saudi led coalition and their allies on the ground. And the Iran conflict at some point did provide them with an opportunity. On the other side of the coin the Iranians also they don't control the Houthis. The Houthis they have influence on the Houthis but the Houthis are not really their proxy. So, there is a limit to Iranian influence on the Houthis but again the timing of Houthi escalation worked pretty well for Iran because this is a period that Iran is trying to make sure that energy prices will remain high if not go higher and the pressure that the Houthis have put on the Red Sea and especially Bab el-Mandeb where about 5 million barrels of Saudi oil exports were going to the Asian markets is pretty beneficial to the Iranians in addition to the fact that again they use the spangled war to mobilize some of their allies in Iraq to fire onto the East-West pipeline which is a pipeline that takes about 3 to 5 million barrels of Saudi oil from the eastern province where it's produced to the Yanbu port on the Red Sea where it could be then exported basically circumventing the Strait of Hormuz that Iran now controls. So, you see that there is alignment of interest, there is certainly a a of cooperation, provision of support for the Houthis by the Iranian. But again, it's also not like the Iranians will push a button and the Houthis will do whatever the Iranians want. In fact, I hear from Iranian sources that they're not very happy with the way the Houthis stretched themselves out too much in this conflict. They conquered territory that they could not hold, especially around Bab al-Mandab, because that's a very flat coastal area in which they would be very much exposed. And they are also against the Houthis conducting attacks against civilian targets like the Riyadh airport. But again, you know, the Houthis don't necessarily listen. I had a colleague who covered Yemen for us, Peter Salisbury, who always had, I thought, the best formulation on Iran-Houthi relations, which was that Iran has, often with the Houthis, it has its foot on the accelerator. It doesn't necessarily have its foot on the brake. >> Mhm. So, let's double back for a moment here, because I am curious to understand what effect this war, and let's talk more specifically about the war since Operation Epic Fury. What effect has it had on Iran? Its economy, its society, how has it accelerated trends that were already in place in the country, etc. >> So, that's a very big question because it has had a lot of different impacts across the board. Let's start maybe politically. I remember talking to about a dozen Iranian officials, former officials, experts at the Doha Forum last December. So, this is after the 12-day war that Israel launched against Iran in June of 2025, and the US joined briefly bombing Iraq's nuclear facility. And everyone agreed that Iran was in a state of absolute dead end, politically, economically, socially. And all of these interlocutors were telling me that they believed that change would have to come. Something's got to give, but they all admitted that this change can only come when the supreme leader dies. So, everybody was waiting for Ali Khamenei to be removed from the scene so that change could come to Iran. So, that was a system that I had described in the past as the Soviet Union in the early 1980s. A system that is at a dead end, is unable to reform itself, but it's not yet at a point of collapse. What the war did is that it removed several layers of top political and military leadership and replace them with some new figures, and it basically made the system much more efficient in making bold decisions in a way that it wasn't under an 86-year-old supreme leader who was set in his ways. Socially, there was, according to surveys that were conducted inside Iran prior to the conflict, about 70 to 80% of the Iranian people who wanted to see fundamental changes. There was a high degree of discontent politically, economically with the system. If you remember, there was a massive protest in January of this year that the regime brutally crushed. But, what the war did is that it almost changed these dynamics in the opposite direction in the sense that the anger that was primarily aimed at the regime is now shared between the regime and the United States and Israel. The hope within many inside Iran that help would come from the outside, whether it's in the form of US or Israeli military intervention, or that it will come from Iranian exiled opposition, is also completely dashed because of, primarily I would say, President Trump's own narrative, which was, you know, pretty hostile towards the nation-state, the threat of civilizational erasure, that kind of language really turned off a lot of Iranians. And these dynamics also energize the regime's core constituents and social base in ways that they were not, even ideologically. It validated the regime's narrative because Iran Islamic Republic used to say that the animosity of the US and Israel towards Iran was against the nation-state and not just against the regime. And people didn't believe it until President Trump demonstrated that animosity is against the nation-state because he wanted to break Iran as a country, not just the regime. So, you had the regime mobilizing its core constituents to come to the public squares throughout the country consistently for almost, you know, 8 months, which is quite something. And you could not have imagined this prior to the conflict. Economically, the situation was dire even before the war. It is now absolutely horrendous. Inflation is above 100%. Unemployment, which was a chronic problem, is now even worse because some of the damage to the infrastructure has pushed literally millions of people out of jobs. For instance, a steel manufacturing factory was targeted, which not only that factory itself, but also the derivative products that it will produce for other industries, it has resulted in unemployment problem becoming way worse. Currency has lost 50% of its value since the beginning of the war. So, I mean, it's a whole litany of economic problems, which has significantly increased the pressure on the population, and the regime does not hesitate to transmit that pressure to the population as long as it can protect the institutions that are essential for its own survival, including, of course, security forces. So, those are the, you know, political, social, and economic dimensions. Of course, there is a lot more to say on geopolitics and on the military, but I'll I'll pause here to see which dimension you want to explore next. >> Well, I am curious how this war has affected the region's geopolitics and the security architecture. So, rather than ask you a question, why don't you Why don't you finish what you were going to say, and then I'll follow up with some additional questions. >> So, I would say the two most important geopolitical effects of this war are number one, the fact that Iran used a point of leverage granted to it by geography, which is the Strait of Hormuz, as means of putting pressure on the global economy. Now, we had seen the Houthis in Yemen putting pressure on the Red Sea, but the implications were so much more limited than what happened on the first day of this conflict, where Iran immediately interrupting traffic in the strait. Shutting down the strait is not really the correct word, because at least for the first 2 months, the Iranians were exporting their own oil to China. There was selective passage that was allowed. They didn't physically blockade the strait. They did selective attacks to basically scare off everybody else and jack up insurance premiums and so on. So, that was the main means of controlling the strait, but it also is fundamentally a new phenomenon, because if you think of the cost that the US has been forced to shoulder in other complex and prolonged conflicts, I wouldn't necessarily call them forever wars, but, you know, from Vietnam to Afghanistan to Iraq, these countries created costs for the United States by bogging it down, high number of casualties, high military expenditure, and so on. But, they were not really able to put pressure on the pocketbook of every American citizen. They were not able to put pressure on, you know, any European, any Australian, any anyone in the global south who would go to a gas station to fill up their tank. This is the first time that a country that is subject to economic coercion by great powers is able to squeeze the global economy in response. And that is something, you know, again, everybody was aware of Iran's ability to shut the strait. I think everybody underestimated of what that really means if Iran does so in practice. And even, you know, until June, July, August, when the US was bombing the southern shoreline of Iran and was considering putting boots on the ground, there was still consideration of the fact that maybe there is a solution of removing Iran's control over the strait. But, as we have seen, it hasn't worked. Even when there are periods that there's a little bit more optimism that more oil is leaking out of the strait, the Iranians find new ways of going after shuttles or supertankers even beyond the strait in the Persian Gulf or in the Sea of Oman and so on. So, that I think is what has been one of the most fundamental effects of this conflict. The second I would say, and that is still a little too soon to judge, but we've seen some evidence for it. Depending on the trajectory of the conflict, it might have longer-term implications. Which is what I call the reverse of the Ukraine phenomenon in the sense that in the war in Ukraine, the West realized that Ukraine could be a bulwark against Russia. That a country that everybody expected would be invaded in in several weeks and the government would fall and then people were thinking about, you know, what kind of insurgencies you can have to combat the Russian invasion, has actually managed to stand its ground and punch back and is doing the fighting for everybody else. And now, Ukraine has been very costly for the West, but the cost is not the same as fighting Russia directly. And it's the same thing that I think Russia and China are not thinking about Iran. That at with very little investment, providing Iran with some intelligence, satellite imagery, electronic warfare capabilities, or even conventional weapons, they have been able to bog down the mightiest military power in the world in the Middle East. And the US has lost tremendous amount of assets, especially interceptor munitions, that could be used in defense of Ukraine, in defense of Taiwan, and so on. And those are very beneficial achievements again to Beijing and Moscow at very low cost. So, that's the second, I think, long-lasting effect of this conflict. >> How much of a toll has the war taken on America's ability to protect its forces and its allies in the region? You know, we've heard a lot about how it's depleted US inventories for Patriot and THAAD missile defense system interceptors. But, what do we actually know concretely? >> Well, look, the problem is that the Pentagon is not going to reveal the exact numbers of how much it has in its stocks. You know, it's often referred to as magazine depth of, you know, how many interceptors there left. But, expert community in DC have been looking at these numbers in terms of production versus how many missiles were shot down, and how many THAAD or Patriots usually used for shooting down a ballistic missile or cruise missile. I have some estimates, and you have to remember that this was not just a one-dimensional conflict. The US was providing some of the same technology to Israel, to the Gulf states. They even moved some of the assets from East Asia to the region and the numbers indicates that about 70% of THAAD missiles have been depleted and around 50% of Patriot missiles and about 75% of the long-range the US ballistic missiles have been depleted. They were used in attacks against Iran. Now, the problem is that it takes a long time for some of these to be produced. They're not easily replaceable and you know, it's not a matter of a few weeks or a few months, it's a matter of a few years. And you know, my sense is that in the medium term, probably the US would learn some very valuable lessons from this conflict and it would fight wars actually much more like the Iranians. It would fight it in asymmetric ways. It would not use a $100,000 interceptor to shoot down a $5,000 drone. It would use some of the cheaper technology that the Ukrainians for instance have produced or it would actually use extensively very similar technology to what the Iranians have produced. We know that the US has already imitated the Shahed drone missile technology and has even used it against Iran. So, in the medium term, I think again, the picture would be different. What is a source of concern for a lot of security experts is the short run. What could happen in the next year or two and how the US would be pretty unprepared for additional black swans that could emerge on you know, geopolitically at the international level. The other effect which again, I think is is very significant is the fact that the US has been kicked out of the region militarily. If you look at all the bases in the Gulf states, in Iraq, in Syria, most of these bases were targeted. We have about 17 US bases that were targeted. Some of them are completely inoperative and would require significant investment to get them back up and running. And I don't think it makes even a lot of sense to rebuild them given the fact that not only they didn't deter an Iranian attack, they invited attacks on themselves and on the territory that was hosting them, mostly the Gulf states. And they would remain vulnerable to the same technology that Iran has. So, does it really make sense to rebuild them? But the fact that you think that US had to accumulate a lot of its military assets in Jordan, and even in Jordan the Iranians conducted a preemptive strike in September that killed several Americans, and the US couldn't defend its base. And so now it has to basically withdraw all the way to Israel. Israel becomes sort of this huge depot of US military assets. But the fact that a third-rate military could kick out a superpower from the region, it's quite stunning. And if you believe that the Iranians were involved one way or another in a potential attack on a US base in the UK, which resulted in the US withdrawing its B-1 fighter jets back to the homeland, it also again tells you that there are serious limitations in how the US military might could basically throw itself around the region and the world when you have the asymmetric warfare tactics that are becoming more and more popular. And by the way, people are learning from each other. You know, if indeed the Iranians were trying to attack the US base in in the UK with drones that were imported into the UK and operated by operatives affiliated with Iran from inside British territory, this is exactly the kind of spider web operation that the Ukrainians conducted against Russia the last year. And again, the Iranians have learned that lesson. So, again, it gives you a lot of insight into what the new kind of warfare is and what are some of the limitations that the United States has despite its military powers to fight in this new era. >> You mentioned Israel a moment ago. Washington and Tel Aviv were engaged in highly cooperative and coordinated joint operations leading into Operation Epic Fury. Are they still operating with the same level of cross-collaboration or have any fissures emerged due to conflicting goals and public perceptions? >> No, there doesn't seem to be the case that there is as much coordination and cooperation as was the case at the beginning of this conflict. This is a war that Israel and the United States started together, but now Israel is completely sidelined. Part of it, I think, is as a result of the fact that Prime Minister Netanyahu overpromised underdelivered in terms of how easy the conflict with Iran would be. He, as public reporting suggests, had promised that the regime would collapse in a matter of a few days. This is why President Trump didn't take the risk of Iran shutting down the Strait of Hormuz seriously because he thought they wouldn't even get to that point. They would be gone by then. And I think that created a deficit of trust in Israeli assessments and is one of the reasons that Israel was sidelined from the conflict after the ceasefire in April. There's also the possibility that Iranian targeting of Israel was becoming too costly for Israel. You know, this is one of the asymmetries between Iran and Israel is that even at the height of the bombing in Iran, you know, it's quite something when you think about the fact that there were several hundreds different sorties every single day in Iran. A total of about 13,000 attacks. And, you know, in some parts of the country people didn't even feel that there is a war. Or, or you know, my own friends and families, they rarely went into a shelter. Whereas, in Israel every single day 6 million Israelis had to go into shelter because, you know, a small country and it would be affected by a war like this. That has economic implications. That again has implications in terms of munitions that you need to shoot down these missiles. So, it might also reflect a limited capacity for attritional conflict for a state like Israel to fight. But, I also think it is demonstrative of US disappointment in what Israel had sold to the Trump administration as sort of a slam dunk. >> So, actually this is not a question I had prepared or thought about because it's been a while since I've seen videos of Israel being hit with missiles from Iran. But, what exactly is the toll that the country has taken? And when's the last time that that they were attacked? And is there an expectation that the Iranians would continue to attack Israel as a way of gaining concessions out of the US in the course of negotiations in the way that they've targeted Gulf infrastructure as an example? >> Right. So, it's quite interesting because even during the 40-day war, the UAE for instance received more Iranian attacks than Israel did. And when I asked the senior Iranian official to explain this, his point was that, you know, it's just a very simple question of geography. The Gulf states are closer. Israel is a thousand kilometers away. And it is surrounded by a multi-layer air defense system, whereas most of the Gulf states are are vulnerable to Iranian attacks and there is a wider range of targets because the Iranians were even going after data centers or some companies that were affiliated with the Trump organization and so on. Whereas in Israel that kind of targeting becomes more difficult. But the last time Iranians fired on Israel was the end of the 40-day war. So in April and since then there hasn't been any attack despite the fact that Iran and the US have engaged in several rounds of tit-for-tat confrontation. This is I think partly driven by what I mentioned to you that Israel itself understands that there's a limit to what it can do and also a high cost to engage in in a very lengthy fight with Iran. It's better if the US does the dirty job and Israel comes in every now and then. But there's also Iranian reluctance to bring Israel in because unlike President Trump who threatened to target Iranian infrastructure and with the exception of a few cases like some bridges and and railways, he really didn't go after critical infrastructure. Israel was already targeting, as I mentioned to you, steel manufacturing companies, petrochemical companies, and some of the sources of wealth for the Islamic Republic. And that I think is one of the reasons that the Iranians don't necessarily want to reopen the front against Israel. Now push comes to shove, of course, if they are attacked, they will strike back. But my sense is that they would prefer the continuation of the situation in which they're not opening too many fronts at the same time.
